approachQuestion.prompt:
One Badge Exchange

A lowercase string `badges` gives badges in a row. You may swap at most one pair of positions, anywhere in the row. Return the longest contiguous run of equal letters that can exist after the optional swap. Return zero for empty input.

Limits and assumptions:
• 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; badges contains only the 26 lowercase English letters.
• A swap preserves the total number of each letter. Return only a length, keeping the input unchanged.

Examples:
1. badges = "aabaa" → 4, by exchanging b with an endpoint a.
2. badges = "ababa" → 3.
3. badges = "aaaa" → 4.

Choose one approach.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; badges contains only the 26 lowercase English letters.
A swap preserves the total number of each letter. Return only a length, keeping the input unchanged.

options.text: Count the global total of each letter. For each of the 26 target letters, move a window with at most one non-target character. For each valid window consider the smaller of its length and the global target count. Return the greatest result.
options.feedback: One outsider can be swapped with a target outside the window. If no spare target exists, the global count caps the result at the target letters already available.

options.text: Try no swap and every pair of positions, scan each resulting conceptual string for its longest equal-letter run, and return the best.
options.feedback: This exhausts the allowed operation and is correct, but repeats many scans when one-outsider windows and global counts suffice.

options.text: For each letter find the longest segment with at most one different character and return its length without a global count cap.
options.feedback: For "aabaa" this would claim five As after one swap, but only four As exist in the entire string.

options.text: For each letter add all its run lengths anywhere in the string and return the greatest total.
options.feedback: For "abacada", four As occur, but one exchange cannot merge all four separated As into one run; the best length is three.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only “Cap one-outsider windows by supply” as specified in the method reveal. Choose the tightest worst-case running-time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use unit-cost random access and arithmetic on machine words large enough for every index and sum.
Input is read-only and excluded from auxiliary space. The scalar or index-pair output is excluded; no candidate segment is copied.
The implementation is iterative with a constant call stack. No hashing is used; fixed alphabet arrays, when present, are direct indexed.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Exactly 26 linear target-letter sweeps use fixed-alphabet storage.
details: For a window with one outsider and a spare target outside, one swap fills the hole. Without a spare, swapping the outsider with a boundary target gives a run of window length minus one, equal to the global supply cap when all targets are inside. A zero-outsider window already forms a run. Conversely a single swap can create a run whose source span contains at most one outsider and cannot exceed global supply. There are exactly 26 linear sweeps, hence O(n) time and constant storage.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: There are 26 target-letter sweeps, not n target sweeps. Each uses two forward boundaries rather than all substring pairs.
“O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: No sort or per-position table is created; one fixed 26-counter array and per-target scalar state suffice.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The global counts use exactly 26 slots; the current window stores only its boundaries and outsider count.
